question: An 80-year-old man with mild hepatic impairment needs a sedative-hypnotic for acute insomnia. Which agent is MOST appropriate?

answers.text: Lorazepam — no active metabolites, undergoes glucuronidation only (Phase II), which is preserved in hepatic impairment and ageing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Lorazepam bypasses Phase I oxidative metabolism (impaired in elderly and liver disease) and undergoes only Phase II conjugation (glucuronidation), which is relatively preserved. It produces no active metabolites, preventing accumulation.

answers.text: Diazepam — the gold standard anxiolytic-hypnotic with the most clinical evidence

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Diazepam undergoes extensive Phase I oxidative metabolism producing the active metabolite desmethyldiazepam (half-life 36-200 hours), which accumulates dramatically in elderly patients with hepatic impairment. This causes prolonged sedation and increased fall risk.

answers.text: Flurazepam — long duration ensures uninterrupted sleep throughout the night

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Flurazepam produces active metabolites with half-lives exceeding 100 hours. In an elderly patient with hepatic impairment, these accumulate over days, causing excessive daytime sedation, confusion, and falls.

answers.text: Zolpidem — Z-drug with α₁ selectivity avoids all BZD-related problems in the elderly

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While zolpidem has relative α₁ selectivity, it still undergoes hepatic Phase I metabolism (CYP3A4/CYP1A2) and can accumulate in hepatic impairment. The FDA recommends lower doses in elderly. Z-drugs also carry risks of parasomnias (sleep-walking, sleep-driving) in older adults.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key principle: Phase I oxidative metabolism declines with age and liver disease; Phase II conjugation is relatively preserved. BZDs with active metabolites (diazepam, flurazepam) accumulate dangerously in elderly patients.
In elderly patients with hepatic impairment, choose BZDs that undergo Phase II conjugation only (lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam — the 'LOT' drugs) to avoid accumulation of active metabolites.
